transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: Fri Feb 14 2025
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Lowe (Redwood AE), Priya Narang (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SRE), Lena Park (Zenith CTO), Marco Diaz (Zenith ML Platform Lead), Jules Reed (Zenith SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Quick technical deep dive requested by Zenith to validate Redwood autoscale patterns for production inference in a VPC; emphasis on burst handling and reserved capacity sizing.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Marcus: Alright folks we're on the record, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intros real fast, I'm Marcus (AE), Priya's our SE, Ethan's our infra SRE.
[00:00:12] Lena: Hey everyone, Lena here. Marco and Jules with me. We're trying to lock down how Redwood would autoscale for our production traffic and how to size reserved GPUs for predictable cost.
[00:00:22] Priya: Great, thanks. High level agenda: burst policies and queueing, reserved capacity sizing and pricing, KV cache warm pools and hit rates, and then batching/quantization tradeoffs for throughput vs p95 latency.
[00:00:36] Marco: Sounds good. We have a fairly spiky waveform - e.g., daily peaks with occasional sudden 10x bursts from our product experiments. We cannot tolerate p99 > 1s for certain customer flows.
[00:00:48] Ethan: Quick note: we're on a VPC deployment in AWS, with private subnets; no outbound internet for model downloads, so any warm pools have to be prewarmed in VPC or we need an on-prem image.
[00:01:03] Priya: Good callout. So first: burst policies. Redwood supports two complementary approaches: prewarmed instances (dedicated warm pool), and rapid on-demand scale-up with queueing and backpressure policies. Prewarm reduces cold-start and KV cache miss penalties, but costs reserved capacity. On-demand is cheaper but requires careful queueing thresholds and graceful degradation.
[00:01:24] Jules: Can you explain what you mean by "KV cache miss penalties"? We saw earlier that first-request latencies spike.
[00:01:30] Priya: Sure. When a model instance spins up, its KV cache (key-value attention cache for prior tokens) is empty. If you have many parallel sessions with long context, populating that cache causes a burst of compute and memory access which shows up as latency spikes. Prewarming keeps KV cache primed for common prefixes or warm sessions. There's also prefix caching at the request router which helps avoid serializing large prefixes repeatedly.
[00:01:53] Marco: How big a warm pool would we need to handle a 10x sudden spike if we have 8 baseline GPUs?
[00:01:59] Priya: It depends on per-GPU throughput for your model variant. For a rough calc: if one GPU handles 120 concurrent low-latency streams at p95 target and you expect 10x burst, you need ~9 GPUs (8 baseline + 8 extra) — but that's naive. We usually recommend a hybrid: reserve a small warm pool sized for typical burst percentile (p90-p95) and allow on-demand to handle rarer spikes, with a short queueing window and token-aware backpressure.
[00:02:24] Marcus: Also we have baked-in burst policies: short lived "burst buckets" which can burst above reserved capacity for up to N minutes. Those map to Redwood's burst capacity config where you set a burst duration and max concurrent extra GPUs.
[00:02:36] Lena: We need to balance cost. Reserved GPUs cost monthly; bursting costs are pay-as-you-go but can blow up. Any heuristics you recommend?
[00:02:44] Ethan: We also have regulatory requirement to limit models serving PII to private cluster. So any bursting that spins up in other regions is not acceptable.
[00:02:52] Priya: For cost control, we recommend: 1) model-level priority policies (critical flows pinned to reserved pool), 2) conservative warm-pool sizing to cover p90 bursts, 3) set a maximum burst budget per day/week, and 4) implement queue admission controls with soft-fail/fast-fail tiers. That prevents runaway egress costs.
[00:03:11] Marco: Ok. What about queueing models — FIFO vs priority queuing?
[00:03:16] Priya: Redwood supports priority-based queues. We suggest multi-class queues: high-priority short-context interactive requests with tight SLOs; medium-priority async requests tolerating up to X seconds; low-priority background jobs (batch reranks). High-priority routes get reserved concurrency. You can configure admission thresholds: e.g., if queue length > 50 for high-priority, trigger auto-scale or degrade to shorter generation lengths.
[00:03:39] Jules: What's the recommended max queue wait time before we offload or reject?
[00:03:42] Ethan: From our experience 200-400ms queueing is tolerable for interactive UIs but not for API contracts.
[00:03:48] Priya: We typically cap queueing at 250ms for strict SLOs and 1s for medium. Above that we either fall back to a smaller model or return a cached answer. Redwood's fallback policies let you route to a quantized variant automatically when queueing crosses thresholds.
[00:04:03] Lena: Speaking of quantization, how does that interact with latency and throughput when autoscaling?
[00:04:08] Priya: Quantized variants often give 1.8-3x throughput improvements depending on model and kernel support, but can increase per-token variance slightly. For autoscaling, using a quantized variant as a fallback is a common strategy to absorb bursts without adding GPUs. But watch quality drop — that's where monitoring and regression alerts come in. Also quantized instances may have different memory footprints, which affects how many concurrent streams fit on a single GPU and thus the autoscaler math.
[00:04:33] Marco: So in practice you'd set primary as full-precision on reserved GPUs and fallback to quantized on burst?
[00:04:37] Priya: Exactly, for user-facing flows where quality matters. For low-cost paths you could run quantized primary.
[00:04:42] Marcus: Let's dig into autoscaler mechanics. Redwood's autoscaler uses a mixture of reactive metrics (CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, tail latency) and predictive signals (short-term request rate forecast derived from request histograms). For VPC/private deployments we also support warm-pools and prewarmed snapshots so instances come up with model and KV cache already initialized.
[00:05:00] Marco: How do prewarmed snapshots work? Do they count as reserved capacity in billing?
[00:05:04] Priya: Prewarmed snapshots are essentially stopped instances with the model loaded and cache warmed, ready to go. In Hosted they live in Redwood infra and billed as reserved capacity when you commit, or as a short-term prewarm fee if you request on-demand. In Private/VPC you manage the prewarmed VMs; Redwood's control plane tracks and recommends sizes but billing depends on your infra.
[00:05:23] Jules: For our VPC we prefer not to keep many prewarmed instances running overnight. Any ideas on lifecycle management to reduce cost but keep p95 stable?
[00:05:31] Priya: Use adaptive warm pools: keep a small base set always on, plus a warm-standby group that is only spun to warm snapshots during predictable windows (e.g., morning launch). Also use model sharding to reduce per-instance memory pressure so more streams fit, and request routing that groups similar contexts to reuse cached KV regions.
[00:05:51] Marcus: Also TTL-based eviction on cache entries — if you can accept shorter context history, eviction reduces memory footprint and speeds startup.
[00:05:58] Marco: One of our constraints: single-tenant GPU pools for compliance. If we reserve ten GPUs, can Redwood autoscale above that into shared-hosted pool in emergency?
[00:06:07] Priya: If tenancy restrictions forbid sharing, we can't spin up hosted shared GPUs. However we can enable cross-account reserved pools inside your VPC if you want Redwood to provision additional instances into your account on demand. That becomes an infra provisioning problem (IAM/AMI) but it's doable.
[00:06:22] Lena: Okay. Let's talk numbers. We'll share 30-day histograms but can you give a sample sizing methodology?
[00:06:28] Priya: Sure — stepwise: 1) Compute target concurrency per GPU: tokens/sec * average tokens-per-request / model throughput. 2) Choose SLO headroom: e.g., reserve 20% extra capacity for p95 headroom. 3) Define warm pool covering p90 bursts. 4) Set burst cap for rare spikes with cost budget. 5) Add fallback quantized variant and short queue thresholds. We'll send an example spreadsheet.
[00:06:52] Marcus: And queueing model: use per-route token budgets so long requests don't starve short ones; also token-aware batching means short requests batch faster.
[00:07:02] Marco: Token-aware batching — can that be tuned per-route? We have some routes with long contexts and some short chat snippets.
[00:07:08] Priya: Yes, per-route batching and max-batch-size plus max-delay settings. For long-context routes keep max-delay low to avoid head-of-line latancy. For short snippets you can increase batch delay to improve throughput and cost.
[00:07:22] Jules: Any gotchas when moving to on-prem? Kernel optimizations, CUDA drivers, etc?
[00:07:27] Ethan: Driver mismatch killed a pilot for us last year.
[00:07:29] Priya: For on-prem we provide a validated AMI/container image and a kernel/driver matrix. Quant kernels sometimes require specific CUDA/cuBLAS versions; we'll share our compatibility doc. Also perf differences across GPU families (A100 vs H100) change concurrency assumptions and batching sweet spots.
[00:07:45] Lena: How do you measure and alert for regressions when we use fallback quantized models? We need to ensure no silent quality drops.
[00:07:52] Priya: Redwood Optimize ties regressions to eval sets. You can define per-route eval prompts and have alerts when embedding similarity or token-level divergences exceed thresholds. Also can tie alerts to human-in-the-loop sampling.
[00:08:05] Marcus: Alright time check — we've been at it 8 minutes; keep going.
[00:08:09] Marco: A few practical scenarios: 1) 10x spike sustained for 3 minutes — prefer warm pool; 2) 3x spike sustained 30 minutes — use on-demand scale with gradual ramp; 3) micro-bursts under 6 seconds — queue + batching often sufficient. Thoughts?
[00:08:25] Priya: That's aligned. For 3) short bursts we rely on token-aware batching; for 1) warm pool sized for p90; for 2) on-demand scale but with a cap and a fallback to quantized. Also setting request-level timeouts and circuit-breakers is important.
[00:08:38] Jules: On the circuit-breaker, do you recommend returning HTTP 429 or a cached answer?
[00:08:42] Ethan: For user-facing flows cached answer or degraded mode is better; for API partners 429 with retry-after is fine.
[00:08:48] Priya: Redwood supports both. You can configure route-level fallback sequences: cache -> quantized -> 429.
[00:08:54] Lena: Ok final part — data residency & audit logs for autoscale actions. We need an audit trail when new instances spin up and what model variants served requests.
[00:09:02] Priya: Audit logs are available; for private deployments logs can be pushed to your SIEM via syslog/Kinesis. We log model version, instance id, route id, and the autoscale trigger reason.
[00:09:14] Marcus: Great. Quick recap before close: Priya will share the autoscaling runbook, driver matrix, and a sample spreadsheet; Marcus will send reserved GPU pricing and recommended warm-pool sizes; Marco will provide histograms and queue metrics.
[00:09:29] Lena: That works. Any blockers?
[00:09:31] Marco: Not from me. We'll prioritize getting histograms by Monday.
[00:09:35] Marcus: Perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and link the docs.
[00:09:40] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[00:09:41] (call ends)
